and below the axis with opposite signs, so inversion through the centre swaps a positive lobe

**(3) σ-antibonding orbitals are gerade** ✗ wrong — σ* is **ungerade**; it is σ *bonding*
that is gerade.

When two atomic orbitals combine, one **bonding** molecular orbital is formed below the atomic
level and one **antibonding** molecular orbital above it. The two shifts are **not equal**.
The antibonding orbital is **raised by more** than the bonding one is lowered ✓ — which is
exactly what statement (c) says.
The reason is internuclear repulsion. In the bonding orbital the electron density piles up
**between** the nuclei and screens them from each other. In the antibonding orbital there is a
**node** between the nuclei, so the density is pushed to the outside, the two nuclei are left
facing each other unscreened, and that extra repulsion pushes the antibonding level further
up than the bonding level went down.
The consequence matters, and is the reason the question is asked:
if a bonding and an antibonding orbital are **both** filled, the net effect is **destabilising**,
not neutral.
That is why **He₂ does not exist**. Its four electrons fill σ1s and σ*1s, and although the
bond order works out to zero, the molecule is actually *less* stable than two separate atoms.
The same argument explains why Ne₂ and Be₂ are not found.
Option (a) is the common misconception — a symmetrical diagram — and the answer here is the
correction to it.
∴ BMO is lowered by less energy than ABMO is raised.

Work out the valency of each element from its valence electrons, then combine them.
**Element A** has **3** valence electrons. Three is fewer than four, so A will **lose** them
to reach a noble-gas configuration: A forms **A³⁺**, valency **3**. (This is group 13 —
aluminium.)
**Element B** has **6** valence electrons. Six is more than four, so B will **gain** two to
complete its octet: B forms **B²⁻**, valency **2**. (This is group 16 — oxygen or sulphur.)
**Combine them so the charges cancel.** The compound must be electrically neutral:
x(+3) + y(−2) = 0
The smallest whole numbers that work are x = 2, y = 3, giving
**A₂B₃** ✓
The shortcut is the familiar **criss-cross** rule: write the valency of each element and swap
them as subscripts — A with valency 3 and B with valency 2 give A₂B₃.
Check: 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6, which cancel ✓
Real examples confirm the formula: Al₂O₃, Al₂S₃, B₂O₃ — all A₂B₃ compounds of a group-13
element with a group-16 element.
∴ A₂B₃.

each orbital, all spins parallel — is unusually stable, because the arrangement is
spherically symmetrical and carries the maximum exchange energy. 4f has seven orbitals, so
4f⁷ is exactly half full. Gadolinium gains more from keeping that half-filled set intact than
it would from putting the 64th electron into 4f, so that electron goes into the 5d orbital
instead.

metals, and lutetium (4f¹⁴5d¹6s²) at the other end of the lanthanoids, where the f subshell is
completely full.

lanthanoids, which is why gadolinium compounds are used as MRI contrast agents.

In the long form of the periodic table the **period number** is the number of the outermost
shell being filled — that is, the **maximum principal quantum number (n)** reached by any
element in that period ✓
Take examples:
**Period 2** — Li 2s¹ through Ne 2s²2p⁶. The highest n is **2**.
**Period 3** — Na 3s¹ through Ar 3s²3p⁶. The highest n is **3**.
**Period 4** — K 4s¹, then the 3d series Sc–Zn, then Ga–Kr filling 4p. Note that the 3d
electrons have n = 3, but the **maximum** n reached in the period is **4**, from the 4s and 4p
electrons — which is why the period number is 4 and not 3.
That last case is exactly why the definition says *maximum*: in the d-block the subshell being
filled belongs to shell (n−1), so counting the filling subshell would give the wrong answer.
Now the distractors:
(a) The **magnetic** quantum number m describes an orbital's orientation and takes values
from −l to +l; it has nothing to do with the period.
(b) The **atomic number** rises steadily down the table and is never equal to the period.
(d) The **azimuthal** quantum number l identifies the subshell (0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d) and
never exceeds 3, so it could not number seven periods.
∴ maximum principal quantum number of any element of the period.

The last element of the **p-block** in any period is the **noble gas** that closes it, because
the p subshell is then completely filled.
In the **6th period** that element is **radon**, Z = 86.
Build its configuration. The 6th period fills in the order 6s, then 4f, then 5d, then 6p:
Rn = [Xe] **4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶**
Check the count: 54 (xenon core) + 14 + 10 + 2 + 6 = **86** ✓
The outermost configuration asked for is therefore **4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶**, option (c).
Now the others:
(a) 7s² 7p⁶ would be the **7th** period — oganesson, Z = 118, not radon.
(b) 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7s² 7p⁰ also belongs to the 7th period, and 7p⁰ means the p subshell is empty,
so it could not be the *last* p-block element.
(d) 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁴ has only four p electrons — that is polonium, two places short of the
end of the block.
The general rule: the last p-block element of period n has the configuration ns² np⁶, with
whatever d and f subshells that period has also filled.
∴ 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶.

Note: the printed key gives (a). 7s² 7p⁶ is the 7th-period noble gas, not the 6th; radon ends
the p-block in period 6, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (c).

**Step 1 — build the configuration of element 114.** The 7th period fills 7s, then 5f, then

7s² takes us to 88
5f¹⁴ takes us to 102
6d¹⁰ takes us to 112

**[Rn] 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7s² 7p²** ✓ (86 + 2 + 14 + 10 + 2 = 114 ✓)
**Step 2 — find the group.** The outermost shell holds 7s² 7p², that is **four** valence
electrons, so element 114 belongs to **group 14** — the **carbon family**, below lead.
That is option **(a)**.
The element is now named **flerovium (Fl)**, and it was expected to be relatively long-lived
because 114 protons lie near the predicted 'island of stability'.
The other options can be eliminated on the valence count alone: the oxygen family (b) would
need 7p⁴ (Z = 116), the nitrogen family (c) 7p³ (Z = 115) — and the configuration printed
against it, 7p⁶, is a noble gas, not group 15 — and the halogen family (d) 7p⁵ (Z = 117).
(The book prints option (a) as 6f¹⁰; that is a misprint for **6d¹⁰** — there is no 6f subshell
in this part of the table — and it does not affect the reasoning, since the group is fixed by
the 7p² ending.)
∴ carbon family, [Rn] 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7s² 7p².
